newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader seeks to outflank opponents.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader seeks to outflank opponents.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko, tightening his grip on Belarus, prepared on Wednesday to push his opponents out of the parliament building using painters and electricians rather than riot police.

Belarus has had two rival parliaments since Lukashenko's victory in Sunday's referendum, pronounced illegal by Europe's top human rights body, but on Wednesday the balance of power swung further in the president's favour.

Facing defiance from a rump of several dozen deputies who are occupying the old parliament and ignoring his plans to form two houses, Lukashenko's supporters made clear he would try to get them out by renovating their workplace.

"The president has promised to create working conditions for the two chambers. We must ask his administration to renovate the Oval Hall urgently," deputy Yuri Pashkevich told 114 pro- Lukashenko deputies meeting in a separate building.
Opposition deputies had expressed fears that Lukashenko might get them out by force, as in April 1995, when hunger-striking deputies were beaten out of the chamber.
Pashekevich's remarks suggested that the rump of the old parliament might soon be barred from the hall by closing it for redecoration -- a trick frequently used in the old Soviet Union.
Deputies loyal to the president pressed ahead on Wednesday with the formation of a new, 110-seat lower house, to be followed later by an upper house with 64 members.

Meanwhile the screws tightened on the old parliamentary leadership. Newspapers published the text of Lukashenko's new constitution, which was declared to be now in force, stripping the old Supreme Soviet of its constitutional role.

An aide to speaker Semyon Sharetsky, whose rump parliament was recognised by a Council of Europe delegation on Wednesday as the legal one, told Reuters that special phone lines linking the chamber to the president and the government had been cut.
"A violent solution would not suit the president," said liberal deputy Anatoly Lebedko after a closed session during which they created a union to oppose Lukashenko's constitution.
But the chairman of a Council of Europe delegation, Tadeusz Iwinski of Poland, warned Belarus at a news conference in the old parliament that it should be ready for anything.

"The worst case scenario would be the use of force...but the best scenario would be to introduce the rule of law," he said after declaring the referendum illegal and saying the new constitution "fell short of minimum democratic standards".
Asked what he could realistically hope for in the next few days, he said: "We should be prepared for different scenarios."

Iwinski, whose delegation was invited by Sharetsky, said they had met Lukashenko for two hours and told him Belarus could join their pan-European body which promotes democracy and human rights as soon as he met its standards.
He said the conversation "instead of dialogue, consisted of two monologues".
Lukashenko told his visitors democracy in Belarus was at a more mature stage than it was in France.
"I replied: Mr President, unfortunately there is nobody among us from France. But I am forced to defend French democracy," Iwinski said.

Russia, Belarus's most powerful ally and its biggest creditor for oil and gas deliveries, has signalled it will accept Lukashenko's new constitutional order providing there is no violence against his opponents.

The Kremlin sent a clear message of support to Minsk on Wednesday when it despatched Defence Minister Igor Rodionov to a ceremony to mark the withdrawal to Russia of the last Soviet-era nuclear missile on Belarussian territory.
Aides to Lukashenko, who will formally sign the new constitution at an official ceremony on Thursday, said the president would not attend the missile withdrawal.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, whose summit in Lisbon next week will be attended by Lukashenko, said it was sending its secretary-general Giancarlo Aragona to Minsk to explore the situation.
